live.name: MageCart
live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: web skimmers that steal card details at online checkouts
next.in_short: MageCart is the name for attacks that plant JavaScript on shop checkout pages to copy card details. Reports describe many groups, thousands of sites, and victims from retailers to restaurants.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card information from compromised eCommerce websites.
Trend Micro says multiple groups are using the Magecart code, which it describes as a piece of malicious JavaScript.

Headlines in Malpedia's reference list name several groups or clusters under the Magecart label, including Group 4, Group 8, Group 12, Keeper, Mirrorthief and ATMZOW. One headline ties FIN6 to Magecart skimmers.
WIRED reported in July 2019 that Magecart hackers were casting the widest possible net to find vulnerable ecommerce sites.
Trend Micro named victims across several sectors, including Newegg, Target, Home Depot and Ticketmaster. It also cited online campus stores serving nearly 200 universities in the US and Canada.
One headline in Malpedia's list reports campaigns that infected 311 restaurants through online ordering platforms.
Malpedia says the first stage is typically JavaScript on a compromised checkout page. It copies data from input fields and sends it to command and control servers.

Malwarebytes described skimmers where compromised shop sites get a single line of code that loads a remote script. The script overlays a rogue iframe on the payment form and sends the stolen data back in encoded form.
Malwarebytes also reported that the attackers hosted skimmer infrastructure on Heroku, and that the abusive instances were reported and taken down.

Trend Micro lists three tactics: infecting third-party companies that supply code to other sites, scanning the internet for unsecured servers, and writing skimming code that works across many payment pages.
A report on Volusion says most Magecart attacks use vulnerabilities in self-hosted stores to plant skimmer code.
Sucuri described the ATMZOW skimmer, planted through Google Tag Manager containers. In late 2023 its operators used base64 encoding and a list of 40 newly registered domains hidden behind a firewall.
RiskIQ reported that Magecart operators registered a lookalike domain on August 13th, 2018. The skimmer went live on Newegg's payment page around August 14th and was removed on September 18th.
RiskIQ said the Newegg skimmer code was recognisable from the British Airways incident.
WIRED reported in 2019 that the group had hit 17,000 domains in a few months. It named British Airways and Ticketmaster among past hacks.
Trend Micro cited a separate attack in which 962 online stores were hit in 24 hours.

In October 2019 hackers breached Volusion, which hosts online stores, and altered a file so shoppers' card details were captured. The report said more than 6,500 stores were affected and the number could be higher.
Sucuri advises site owners to treat unexpected scripts as signs of compromise.
Trend Micro notes that blocking untrusted JavaScript would not prevent exposure if a trusted site is itself compromised.
Shoppers can check card statements regularly and report unfamiliar charges to their bank quickly.
